summary:
Johor stands under the national framework of Malaysia, which criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code punish same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping; the offences apply to men and women alike, reach conduct regardless of consent, and are not limited to Malaysian citizens, so they bind visitors. Sodomy was first criminalised in 1871.

Every one of the 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya, Johor included, maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only; enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the provisions contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. State Sharia codes separately criminalise same-sex intimacy for Muslims.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court refused a request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. No comparable ruling has dismantled Johor's own cross-dressing provisions on record. A constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Johor has moved in a punitive direction in its own right. In November 2023 the state government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people. Public-morality offences in the state are enforced through its religious authorities, and no protective or tolerant regime specific to Johor is on record.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and publicly staged across the country. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection. State-conducted investigations documented by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, with a crackdown running since the 2018 election; Johor was not among the units named in that survey, which does not indicate an absence of enforcement there.

Queue-and-venue raids carry acute exposure risk. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media were pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details were leaked; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence and official indifference to it. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself". Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects. There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, Johor's Sharia cross-dishing offences do not apply, but the federal Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing rather than individual stops. A visitor attending a sauna, club, screening or any queue-based event assumes the exposure profile of the 28 November 2025 operation, and conversion-therapy or "rehabilitation" measures announced in Johor are directed at residents rather than foreign nationals.
tangentialFactors:
The federal and state layers are legally distinct and move independently. The Federal Court's February 2021 ruling on Selangor's section 28 and its February 2024 ruling on 16 Kelantan provisions rested on federalism grounds, removing state-law overreach while leaving sections 377A to 377D untouched. A visitor therefore gains nothing from a state-level exemption: the Penal Code follows them across every Malaysian state and territory.

The state-conducted investigations recorded by Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters as of August 2022 covered seven units — Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah — under a crackdown running since the 2018 election. Johor was not among them. Comparable reporting on Johor concentrates on the November 2023 announcement of conversion-therapy centres, so the two sources illuminate different mechanisms of the same national climate rather than contradicting each other.

Raids are timed for publicity rather than executed quietly. The Chow Kit operation of 28 November 2025 was pre-tipped to media and produced leaks of detainees' faces, names and official positions, with 17 civil servants suspended; a similar raid followed in Penang within a week. The practical harm is outing and loss of employment and immigration standing, which outlasts any single detention.

Regional comparison is limited. The Federal Court decisions are internal to Malaysia's own division of powers, and no source here establishes how Johor's provisions compare in penalty or practice with neighbouring jurisdictions.
localsOnly:
Johor residents who are Muslim fall under the state Sharia enactment prohibiting cross-dressing and posing as the opposite sex, punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning, enforced by the state religious authorities. Because the provisions define no legal test for transgender dressing, the exposure is open-ended rather than tied to a specified act.

The November 2023 announcement of conversion-therapy centres is a resident-facing measure: government-funded "rehabilitation" infrastructure has no stated application to foreign nationals, though it forms part of the environment a long-term or returning resident encounters. National mukhayyam retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021 under the crackdown running since the 2018 election.

Residents have no statutory recourse against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation: Malaysia has no anti-discrimination law and no same-sex marriage or partner recognition. Documentation of a trans woman's killing in Klang on 25 June 2019 — the third such killing in under two months — records police mistreatment and impunity, indicating that formal complaint routes have produced neither protection nor accountability in documented cases.

Where state Sharia provisions have been struck down, the finding turned on federalism rather than on constitutional rights. Muslim residents in Johor thus retain the full force of their state's enactment while residents of Selangor and Kelantan lost theirs.
